summary: Presents a technique for using XML as the source format when writing Internet-Drafts and RFCs. Authors write structured XML and tools produce the final text. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 7749.

eli5.summary: Instead of typing a document by hand with careful spacing, writers fill in a tagged template, and a program turns it into the finished page.

questions: how to use xml for internet drafts
subtitle: Use XML source to write structured Internet-Drafts and RFCs, with tools to produce text and HTML.

tldr.problem: RFC authors had to carefully format documents by hand using plain text with specific spacing and layout rules, which was tedious and error-prone.
tldr.mechanism: XML markup provides a structured way to tag content elements (sections, lists, references) and a tool converts the XML source to RFC-compliant text and HTML formats automatically.
tldr.outcome: Authors can focus on content while tools handle formatting and layout, ensuring consistency with RFC standards. This RFC was replaced by RFC 7749.

today: RFC 2629 was replaced by RFC 7749, which updated the xml2rfc specification with additional markup elements and features for the modern RFC authoring process.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2629 introduces xml2rfc, a technique for using XML (Extensible Markup Language) as the source format for Internet-Drafts (I-Ds) and RFCs. The RFC has three main goals: define a simple XML Document Type Definition (DTD) that captures RFC formatting requirements while allowing meaningful markup of content structure; describe software that processes these XML files to produce RFC-compliant text and HTML; and provide proof of concept by using the technique to write the RFC itself.

The approach allows authors to use familiar text editors while gaining the benefits of structured markup. Information can be organized, searched and retrieved using both unstructured and structured mechanisms, and the output follows RFC 2223 standards automatically.
sections.eli5: XML is a way to mark up content so computers understand what each part is for—like a title, a list, or a reference—instead of hoping the spacing looks right.

sections.title: XML Basics and Document Structure
sections.content:
An XML document starts with a declaration and a reference to the DTD (Document Type Definition), followed by the root <rfc> element. The key concepts are: an element consisting of a start tag, content and an end tag (e.g., <section>...</section>); an empty element that combines start and end in one tag (e.g., <date/>); attributes on tags that specify properties (e.g., title='Introduction'); and entities like < to represent special characters.

All elements must be properly matched and nested—a tag that opens must close, and nested tags cannot overlap. The document is case sensitive and must escape < and & characters as < and & respectively.
sections.eli5: XML uses angle-bracket tags to label different parts of content—like putting labels on a filing cabinet's drawers so you know what goes where.

sections.title: Front Matter and Metadata
sections.content:
Every RFC starts with a <front> element containing metadata and document headers: a <title> (with optional abbreviation for long titles over 42 characters), one or more <author> elements with initials, surname and fullname attributes, a <date> with month and year, optional <area> elements for IETF categories (Applications, General, Internet, Management, Operations, Routing, Security, Transport, User), <workgroup> elements identifying producing groups, and <keyword> elements for search terms.

An optional <abstract> and optional <note> elements complete the front matter. Author elements contain an <organization> and optional <address> with postal, phone, facsimile, email and URI sub-elements. The status, copyright notice and table of contents are inserted automatically during processing.
sections.eli5: The front matter is the title page and table of contents—it tells who wrote the document, when, and what it's about.

sections.title: Body Structure and Content Elements
sections.content:
The <middle> element contains the document's sections. Each <section> has a mandatory title attribute and an optional anchor for cross-references. Sections can be nested recursively, and each section contains <t> (text paragraph) elements, <list> elements (with style attribute: 'numbers', 'symbols', 'hanging', or 'empty') and <figure> elements for artwork.

A <figure> groups a <preamble>, a mandatory <artwork> (preserving whitespace), and a <postamble>. The <xref> element cross-references sections, figures or references with a target attribute. The <eref> element references external URIs, and the <iref> element adds index entries.
sections.eli5: The body is organized into sections that can nest inside each other, with text, lists, and diagrams, plus links between different parts.

sections.title: Processing and Output
sections.content:
The <back> element contains optional <references> and appendix <section> elements. References consist of <reference> elements with a <front> and <seriesInfo> elements identifying the RFC or other series.

XML source files are processed by validating parsers (checking against the DTD) and transformation tools. The xml2rfc tool reads the XML and produces both RFC-compliant text output (56 lines per page with 69 characters per line per RFC 2223) and HTML. The text version automatically inserts running headers, page breaks and the required status and copyright text. Authors should validate their XML before processing to catch structural errors.
sections.eli5: A computer program reads the tagged XML, checks that it's valid, and converts it to pretty text and web pages that follow all the RFC formatting rules.
